description: ANDROMEDA VITALITY monitors astronaut health on long space missions. The VitalBand smartwatch tracks heart rate, temperature, SpO₂ and radiation, with instant alerts. A wireless ECG patch monitors the heart, and an ultrasound patch checks heart function and muscle loss. In the medical bay, a tablet and live dashboards help the crew detect problems early.
summary:
Our team built Andromeda Vitality, a health monitoring system for astronauts on long missions, and brought it to life in an interactive 3D spacecraft simulation.

Each astronaut wears the VitalBand, a smartwatch that tracks heart rate, skin temperature, blood oxygen and radiation exposure. Alongside it, a wireless ECG patch keeps an eye on the heart, and a wearable ultrasound patch checks heart function and muscle loss. Every module on the ship has its own radiation sensors, with live readings shown on a screen outside each door. In the medical bay, six dashboards, an ultrasound tablet and AI suggestions help the medical officer understand what's happening and act fast. If something goes wrong, like an irregular heartbeat, low oxygen or a fever, the watch walks the astronaut through one of six step-by-step protocols.

Far from Earth, there's no hospital down the road and no doctor on call in real time. That's the problem we wanted to solve. By linking each astronaut's body with the ship around them, our system spots warning signs early. When a solar storm hits, it shows which rooms are unsafe and guides the crew to the radiation shelter.

Radiation, microgravity and isolation quietly wear down the human body. Guided by NASA's Human Research Program and crew health standards, Andromeda Vitality helps keep astronauts safe on the way to the Moon and Mars, and the same idea could one day bring better care to remote communities here on Earth.
details:
Andromeda Vitality is a health monitoring system that connects every astronaut's body to the spacecraft around them. We brought it to life as an interactive 3D simulation of a spacecraft with six modules: the Main Cabin, Medical Bay, Exercise Area, Sleeping Quarters, Radiation Shelter and Airlock. Three crew members, Aina, Wei Jun and Arjun, live and work on board, and the system watches over all of them at once.

It starts on the astronaut's wrist. The VitalBand is a smartwatch that measures heart rate, blood oxygen (SpO₂), skin temperature, heart rate variability, stress and personal radiation dose. Its screen shows the astronaut's live readings and the radiation level of the room they're in. Two more wearables sit on the body. A wireless ECG patch on the left chest, along the breastbone, records the heart's electrical rhythm through two gel electrodes and sends it wirelessly, with a small green light showing it's transmitting. A wearable ultrasound patch on the front of the thigh, connected to a small control unit clipped at the hip, can image the heart, measure the thickness of the thigh muscle to track muscle loss in microgravity, and detect gas bubbles in the veins after a spacewalk.

The spacecraft itself is also monitored. Every module has its own radiation sensors, and a screen outside each door shows the live dose rate with a clear message such as "Safe to enter" or "Do not enter. Go to the radiation shelter." So an astronaut knows a room is safe before stepping in, and in walk-inside mode the simulation even counts up the dose a person collects as they move around the ship.

All this data comes together in the medical bay on six dashboards. The first shows astronaut health: heart rate, SpO₂, temperature, respiratory rate, ECG, blood pressure, sleep and activity. The second tracks radiation, including each person's dose rate, cumulative dose against the 600 mSv career limit, and organ dose estimates. The third covers the cabin environment: oxygen, carbon dioxide, pressure, temperature, humidity, air particles and water quality. The fourth is the medical record, with crew profiles, medicine stock and expiry dates, equipment readiness and a timeline of medical events. The fifth covers fitness and nutrition, such as exercise sessions, calories, fluid intake, fatigue and bone and muscle checks. The sixth handles mission operations: the communication delay with Earth, data sync status and each astronaut's alert level. A wall-mounted ultrasound tablet shows heart scans with ejection fraction and stroke volume, thigh muscle thickness compared to before the flight, and bubble grading after a spacewalk. An AI suggestions screen reads all of this and offers advice, each point linked to the NASA rule behind it. For example, it flags when the average carbon dioxide level in a module rises above the 3 mmHg limit.

When something goes wrong, the watch takes over. We wrote six protocols into the VitalBand. P1 handles a cardiac arrhythmia and P2 handles hypoxia when SpO₂ drops below 92%; both are emergencies. P3 handles fever or heat strain as a warning. P4 covers a sudden stress spike, P5 slow immune changes and P6 bone loss from too little exercise loading; these three are advisories. Each level has its own pattern of beeps and vibration, so an astronaut can tell how serious it is without looking. The watch screen shows the reading, simple numbered steps and buttons to respond. For an arrhythmia, it asks the astronaut to lie flat, keep their arm still for a clean ECG, and press "I am conscious" within 15 seconds before the alert escalates. For stress, it shows a breathing ring: breathe in for 4 seconds, out for 6. The same alert appears on the medical bay dashboards and in the medical log at that moment, so the medical officer sees exactly what the astronaut sees.

We also built three scenarios to show the system in action. In normal cruise, everyone carries on with their day.In a solar particle event, radiation across the ship rises, every door outside the shelter turns to "Do not enter", the crew moves to the radiation shelter, and information panels around the ship show each room's danger level. In the crew fever scenario, Arjun's temperature climbs, his watch screen flips to an alert, and he's moved to the medical bay bed while the dashboards run the fever protocol.

The main benefit is catching problems early, before they turn into emergencies. On a mission to Mars, a message to Earth can take many minutes each way, so the crew can't wait for a doctor to answer. Andromeda Vitality gives them the information and the steps to act on their own. It also cuts down on guesswork: instead of checking separate devices, the medical officer sees everything in one place. Our hope is that it helps keep astronauts safe on long missions to the Moon and Mars. The same idea could also reach people on Earth who live far from a hospital, such as rural communities, offshore workers or research stations, where wearable sensors and clear guidance could make a real difference.

For tools, we built the simulation with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, using the Three.js library for the 3D graphics and canvas drawing for the live watch screens, dashboards and ultrasound images. We used Claude, an AI assistant, to help us write and refine the code. The VitalBand is designed around real, affordable sensors: the MAX30101 for heart rate and blood oxygen, the MLX90614 for contactless skin temperature, the ADXL345 and MPU6050 for motion, a Grove GSR sensor for stress, and an ESP32 microcontroller to process and send the data. The health values in the simulation are simulated, not taken from real astronauts.

What makes our project creative is that it goes from the wrist to the whole ship in one connected system. Viewers can walk through the spacecraft, watch a door monitor change colour, fly the camera down to an astronaut's wrist to see an alert flash, and then follow that same alert onto the medical bay screens. Instead of just describing the idea, we let people step inside it.

We thought about many factors along the way. Our radiation limits and health thresholds follow NASA-STD-3001 and the risks identified by NASA's Human Research Program. We kept the communication delay with Earth in mind, so the system stores data on board and syncs with mission control when a link is available. To avoid false alarms, the motion sensors confirm that an astronaut is at rest before a heart alert is trusted. The wearables had to be light, comfortable and simple enough to wear every day, with a battery level shown on the watch. Alerts are tiered so that small issues don't cause panic but real emergencies can't be missed. Finally, we decided that the AI only gives advice: the final decision always stays with the crew medical officer.
